title: Mogo Chips
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Cassava boiled in salted water with a little oil until soft, drained and cooled, then fried golden and dusted with chilli powder — made this way in Uganda by a grandmother whose son still asks for them.
longDesc: Mogo is cassava — the word is Swahili, mhogo — and mogo chips are the Indian-Ugandan snack that travelled to Britain and stayed. The method is boil-then-fry, and the cooling between the two stages is what gets them crisp, exactly as with the Ugandan party potatoes in UGA056. The chilli powder and lime finish is the one the diaspora remembers: mogo chips doused in chilli powder and fresh lime, eaten at the roadside.
ingredients: Oil — for the boiling water and for frying; no quantity is given in the source
Red chilli powder, or black pepper powder — no quantity given
steps: Boil plenty of water in a pan.
Add a little oil and salt.
Add the cassava and cook until done.
Heat oil in a kadai and carefully add a few chips at a time.
Fry until light golden and crispy.
Sprinkle with chilli powder or pepper powder, and lime juice and zest if you want the full version.
chefTips: Cool them between boiling and frying. It is the same rule as the Ugandan party potatoes in UGA056 and it is what produces a crust rather than a chip that collapses in the oil.
A little oil in the boiling water, which is specified and unusual. It keeps the pieces from sticking to each other as they soften.
Fry a few at a time. Crowding drops the oil temperature and you get greasy mogo.
Remove the tough central fibres. Fresh cassava has a woody core that has to come out, and a chip with one in it is inedible.
Chilli powder and fresh lime is the finish the Ugandan-Asian diaspora remembers most, and it is worth doing properly rather than just salting them.

A no-deep-fry version exists and works: steam the chips 18 to 20 minutes until a knife goes in easily, toss them hard in a colander to roughen the surfaces while warm, then pan-fry in butter and oil with cumin seeds, garlic, chilli, turmeric and lime.
Only the cassava is quantified in the source. Oil, chilli powder and salt are all given without amounts and nothing here has been estimated.
Cassava must be properly cooked. Boil it through before frying, always.
commonMistakes: Under-boiling, so the inside stays hard.
Salting only and skipping the chilli and lime.
sources: Adapted from Hayley Dhanecha, 'Plain Mogo Chips (East African Style)', Jagruti's Cooking Odyssey — the 1 kilogram of cassava, the boil-in-salted-water-with-a-little-oil step, the drain-and-cool instruction, the fry-a-few-at-a-time method and the chilli or pepper powder finish are all hers. Her headnote gives the Uganda attribution directly: her grandmother would make these simple mogo chips back in Uganda, and her father still loves the recipe. Only the cassava is quantified in that source; oil, chilli powder and salt are given without amounts.

The chilli-and-lime finish and its roadside context are from Evie Raja, 'Ugandan-Asian Food and Identity 50 Years On', The Isis Magazine, 11 December 2022, which names mogo chips doused in chilli powder and fresh lime among the dishes that carry cultural memory for the diaspora. That article gives no quantities.

The no-deep-fry method — steaming 18 to 20 minutes, tossing in a colander to roughen the surfaces while warm, then pan-frying with butter, cumin seeds, garlic, chilli, turmeric and lime — is from Sanjana Modha's 'Chilli-Garlic & Lime Mogo', sanjanafeasts.co.uk, July 2020, written for a British-Indian-East African home.
A Kenyan masala mogo variant exists and makes no Uganda claim; it is not used here.
storage: Boiled cassava keeps 2 days refrigerated before frying. Fry to order.
reheating: A hot oven for a few minutes.
healthBenefits: Cassava is high in carbohydrate, vitamin C and resistant starch.
Boiling before frying means less oil is absorbed than in a raw fry.
Deep-fried, so it is a snack.
culturalNote: Mogo chips are the clearest case of a food that belongs to a community rather than a country: a Swahili root vegetable cut like a British chip, spiced like a Gujarati snack, and remembered as Ugandan by people who left in 1972. That the recipe now lives on British food blogs written by grandchildren is the whole story of that community in one dish.
